author: buchanan_robert
text:
But now I am alone again, and know not where my love hath flown,
Nor hear any more her voice nor see her smiling face again,
I cannot sit still and mourn, but must run out through the streets at noon,

author: cushag
text: The wind blew round the apple trees And rattled along their leaves. The boughs bent down, as if they would kiss the ground, So much were they laden with fruit! Then from the upper branches came A sound like singing, or sweet music made Of many notes which seemed to rise On wings of air to Heavenward, Till the whole orchard was filled With that delicious melody.

Once I remember when my mother sang me a song. It was very sweet and low, like all mothers’ voices are that are singing to their children at night. But it made me feel cold and frightened for some reason or other—a strange feeling that something had gone wrong somewhere, that the world could not be what it ought to be. So when the words were over I did not sing again, but went to bed as quietly as I could, holding up my little hands and rubbing them together gently, trying to think about something else instead of that wild thought that would not leave me alone.

author: buchanan_robert
buchanan_robert
text:
The wind is out of the east, and dark behind clouds
Is driving rain down from the steep mountainsides ;
And on my door steps I hear the patter and splash
Of a little horseman, who runs down the street,
Singing a song about the hills that are up there,
About their streams, and their birds, and flowers, and heather,
Who rides through the night like an arrow of flame,

author: cushag
emily_dickinson
text:
Mary, Mary, what are you doin'?

Where's Johnny? he ain't been here to-day;

He went out to see his friends—he knows not when

The poor little children 'll be hungry again.

I sat up late last night in bed,

To see if all the world could be right.

There was no one but myself to bless,

No love or care, so far as my eyes could descry;

And yet there were some folks that did seem quite happy;

All through the land they smiled and laughed so merrily!

What can it be? What have we not seen,

But do not know what happiness really means ?

author: cushag
text:
Oh, Mary, Mary dear,

You know what's come to pass;

I love my sweetheart better than all else in the world.

She don't go without me to the shop or to the mill,

Though she never works but Sundays and holidays, when we both rest

While others are working like slaves.For her sake, too, I'll work as hard as any one,

And not only that, I mean to keep house with her always,

To please her and save money for her housekeeping ;

Then if old age comes and our strength

author: cushag
emily_dickinson
text:
The day is full of music!
 The birds are singing everywhere;
 They chirp and twitter
 In every hedge; they flit and flash about us, as if nature had given them wings,
 To go about us free, to say their little songs in our hearing.

author: john_keats
text:
All that is good or fair
Is mine; whatever there be,
Whatsoever man or beast,
Whatever flies or trees,
Whichever river flows,
Or mountain snows.

And there was a garden in my life, which I had planned,
    But now is overgrown with weeds,
The seeds that were planted there must surely come to growth,
     For nature will not leave them dead;
Though only as weeds they grow, still they are what once grew,
      They can no more be taken away,
So we’ll watch how those old forgotten dreams unfold,
   How they unfold this day!

author: emily_dickinson
text:
I cannot leave behind me
  My garden at this season;
And when they say it is wrong
  The flowers shall live with reason.
But oh! how can we tear them?
  They were a part of earth's glory;
How can we give them back again
  To dust that had them borrow?

author: emily_dickinson
john_keats
text:
“Oh! where is my ship?” said I; “where’s my friend?
For lo, there comes an old man upon the strand!
To me his faithful promise was made—
‘Come,’ saith he, ‘never more!’”

author: john_masefield
text:
He who can run as well as swim
Can cross an ocean in his time;

The old man came in at last,
But little knew what had come amiss;
And on the way from the door to the hearth,
He left behind him many a tear.

author: john_keats
text:
The time was when I could keep my books
Upon an easy, modest shelf; but now they're on a step-ladder or in boxes
Or piled up high against the wall—and the papers are even worse than the books—
I have no room for new books at all.

author: john_keats
john_masefield
text:
"Here in this room I have been staying,
The whole world seemed so fair and gay
To think that all these things were mine,
These great buildings and broad parks fine!

author: kemp_harry_1883_1960
text:
"He is a gentleman, my son."
His eyes were blue as water and his lips red like blood, but that smile I saw in them was different from any other man.
Even though he looked at us as strangers, I felt something deep inside me draw near him...
and now I know why..."

* * *

The first part seems not to have been written about an old woman and the second one seems to refer to someone who has recently seen a man for the first time (his eyes are described very differently). But they can both refer to the same person. The

"He made no reply; he could not speak so soon.
She put him in a cab, as she had been bidden,
And drove away alone; and now she knew well
That nothing ever more would bring them together."

author: john_masefield
text:
"When I left school a young man full of hope,
With ambition bright in my mind for gold-mines,
How could I know that fate had such a trap set?
That all my life would prove as nought at last.
Now aged sixty-two, with no one near,
All is so wasted, when it might have been."


These two pieces are not so far apart, they were written less than thirty years after each other by the author of "The Silver King," but they seem worlds apart. They express an entirely different point of view towards life and its

author: john_masefield
text:
"I think my mother must have been a fool!
Her whole life was a living hell in toil,
But I can see she did it for us all;
All these years since we're gone from home she sits,
Weeping at night because of what we suffer,
Thinking no doubt that God has called us up together."

author: kemp_harry_1883_1960
text:
It is easy when we are young and strong
To build our ships upon the winds;
But in the end it all comes down to this:
Can you put out to sea alone,
In storm or calm, when others have gone?

author: newman_john_henry_1801_1890
text: "In the days when we used our heads . . ." He took the two poems apart line by line in order to show how they were written, as well as what was being said. First he looked at the rhythm of each poem: The Old Man is written with short lines, while An Old Man’s Advice has long ones. The lines of the first poem are mainly iambic tetrameter (four strong beats per line), while those of the second have mostly anapestic dimeter (two weak beats followed by one strong beat).

Here is my tale about a man who goes down
to his ship, on board which he has lived all his life,
and has married and raised children; now this man
is going to sell his property (which includes an island)
and leave the sea forever. His son comes to him with the
intention of trying to persuade his father not to go away from
his lifelong occupation. The father, however, gives in to his wish,
but begs him as well to try hard never to forget the sea and its ways,
so that when he grows up, he might

author: kemp_harry_1883_1960
text:
I’m going home tomorrow, to be married in
the country church; . . ..

He doesn’t like it here, my son does not. . ..
It is hard on him, he says, being away from
home. . .; oh yes, when his ship comes in,

We shall all go back together to our native shore.

Now, what is this man’s story ? Is he a sailor
who has been taken sick or wounded? What do we
know about his age—we cannot tell? Perhaps the
writer has no time to learn

author: kemp_harry_1883_1960
newman_john_henry_1801_1890
text:
His youth was spent in a most hard captivity;

And when at last to liberty he had attained,

author: robert_frost
text:
“The story is true; I have heard it told to me.”

How long ago did you hear this from whom?

“I do not know that myself, but it is not more than two months since I left Rome. But as for other stories, which are often related by your priests—which would be absurd if they were not so believed—there cannot be many such things in Italy as we read of at Alexandria or Antioch. The truth is, what happened here is enough for us to tell to our children, that they may hold their heads up among men.”

How came it to pass that this man had no care
To clothe himself in woollen garments fair, Or that
his feet were shod in boots of leather? But on all
the other hands his nails were as sharp as spears.

And again, by another poetical hand:

They say he walked through the desert alone; For there was not found an
ass nor camel bone; His food consisted only of water and
of barley-meal; He ate neither beef, nor mutton meat, Nor fish,
nor wheat, nor any sweetbread.

author: newman_john_henry_1801_1890
newman_john_henry_1801_1890
text:
The life I lead is bitter to me in this prison;

For food there is nothing but corn-meal gruel.

I want a change for my pain, so that it may be

allayed.

author: robert_frost
text:
"His wife is dead; but they had no children.
She was a good woman, never ill,
And died without pain. He has worked well all these years—
You see his hands are strong and clean, yet old,—
For thirty pound a year, so far as I know;
And now that she's gone he lives alone,
Sleeping on straw in an outhouse built for hens.
The hen-house stands near his garden where he grows
Turnips and mangolds to eat. This place he got,
For sixty pounds, from a friend

author: stephen_crane
text:
"Here we are. There's two of you; and she needs
The help, because she's worn out with the twins,"
And so they come in. She has lost her mother,
She says, but now that she had been bereft of one
Of them she felt that she could carry on alone.

"Why did you send for me,
To let me know you were sick?
The world's all round about me, and there are no people in sight.

author: robert_frost
text:
"They said that he should be allowed to leave
And follow some other trade; they thought
It would suit his temper to become a labourer
Of some sort—a man who had no heart for anything
But idleness, even if it brought food to his mouth."

The first is from William Cowper; the second from Wordsworth. Both are admirable in their way, but both show that there has been a great deal of misunderstanding about the question whether an idle person can make himself useful or not. If this were so, then we might fairly say that, as long as

author: robert_frost
text:
"Oh, if you knew her face and voice so well!
No one in all this city knows her, she Is not for sale; she keeps no shop or stall—
She isn't on the market at all.
How do we know her? Her own poor hand writes
Our bill of lading and our customs pass,
For when she has the means she does not hide,
But pays her dues to justice in advance.

author: stephen_crane
text:
A song bird and two little birds sat down.
The little birds wanted to sing along with it.
It was then that they learned how hard it is to be a song bird.

author: stothert_james_a
text:
The Three Little Birds
Sat on my fence. 
They looked as though they wanted me.
I said to myself,
"They will soon come after me," 
And I didn't know what to do.

Little Bird,
 I know you are asleep;
 You'll not wake up when I peep.
 Little Bird, I hear your wings beat--
 Can they clap?
 Can one wing snap?
 It is a thing great!

author: stephen_crane
text:
Two little people from the hills.
 On a stone they sat; one was called John and one was named Jack. The rocks were round as pebbles,
 And like water were the stones;
 But not all alike, for there were some smooth and some rough; those that were smooth and glassy Were called Jacobus and Jacobus was his name, For I have heard tell, so say my friends it is true. This stone had been polished long ago When Jesus walked on this earth below. There are many such around the town Wherein I dwell; but none more fair Than the one which

author: stephen_crane
text:
In a tree there lived a hen
 And she laid an egg every day.
 The first it was as big as peas;
 But next time it was no bigger than a bean.

author: stothert_james_a
text:
The Great White One was there — one being of all !
Not many minds — not one great God alone!

There is an infinite Being, and no more;
But every soul of man, however low,

Is a small portion of this All divine,
Which yet remains unmanifested quite.

It only shows us parts of itself;
This is the sense I find within my heart :

Of this I am so certain, that if you

Were to deny, I should refuse your part

author: thomas_hardy
text:
"The very soul of nature seems at once
To melt away and disappear from view ;

The Sun in Heaven and we upon Earth;
These twinly spheres are one; and yet apart.
Two worlds are ours: but when their union's worth
We feel in every breath, and soul expands,
As if she were an angel from her throne
In heaven, where nothing seems so near or far ;

Then do I deem this mortal life a part
Of my eternal being : for they join,
When love makes Nature seem the world beyond

author: stothert_james_a
text:
The heart's great centre was created long ago,
And in an ancient time the mighty powers began to glow :
But these have faded since--the glorious light and heat are gone,
For the great globe, whereon they shone like a star, fell from Heaven.

author: stothert_james_a
text:
"The voice of him whom we seek hath spoken ;
He called us home ; and now a spirit's token
Of heaven's sweet truth, upon our eyes, is spoken :

Our Saviour Jesus Christ ! The world shall know
What glory waits behind its earthly show."

author: thomas_hardy
text:
It seems that my heart is broken,
 But it must be mended soon;
 The world's still full of laughter,
 My brain is never lonely.—

author: william_wordsworth
text:
IN one white spot on the sky
 I saw her face; it was not new.
 Her hair shone white as milk of thyme
 On the pale head that had known dreams;
 Her eyes, like stars at the dawn,
 Shone through a veil of silver beams.

I saw an eagle pass above me,
  His wings in the wind were beating;
And his head dropt down beneath his crest,
      Like some one who cannot be cheating.


A bird of prey was he, I thought him gay,
   The man I met was not so gay.
But I had looked up from what I sought him,
    And thus his air seemed but a play.

author: thomas_hardy
text:
In silence I sit down and think. 

Why was I born? 
It is because I am weak and timid that I ask why? 

I know not what my spirit is, nor do I understand it; but if only I could grasp it, then would I become strong and bold, and all questions would be solved! 

O, that I were like you who can reason on any subject. You are never tired, yet your brain goes ever fresh into new regions, while mine grows weary and becomes feeble after the most trifling thought or effort; for me everything is dead

author: thomas_hardy
text:
I HAVE not seen you for many a day,
But I have heard you; my ears are fed
With news that fills me with gladness;
And when my eyes your image read,
My heart is filled with a sudden glow;
Your voice comes back like an echo
From some long vanished home ago.

author: william_wordsworth
text:
Hail, thou proud, brave, blessed Isle!
 That like the Sun art born to rule!
 Whose radiant face doth fill the skies,
 And bless them all around from pole to pole.
 Hail, thou, whom Heav'n hath made most fair,
 With mountains, woods, and smiling plains,
 Where peace, content, true freedom are,
 From Tyrants free, and Foes in chains,
 The happy home of Liberty,
 O Freedom! queen of States renown'd,
 By many nations for thy pow’r admir'd:
 Thy scept

author: buchanan_robert
text:
I am weary of myself. What an age hath she been! So much has she seen already—so much remains for her to see. The sun is fallen seven times upon her forehead since she was born; but all this while she had slept quietly under its beams, till now she wakes suddenly at length from her long repose, feeling herself grown old, and knows not whether she shall rise or fall. And yet what is there in her? Only a little dust collected along the verge of a great road, which any footstep may tread beneath them.

What is that voice again? It seems

To the Poet

Oft thou dost lift thine eyes in vain To gaze upon the sun, or stars afar.

So do we often turn our looks to find
The bliss which may not be. No more, no less
We see than others when they look at us,
No more nor less we feel ourselves desired.
Each knows his own best happiness, and bears
His portion from that source of light which fills
All space with its incessant flow: for this
We need no other star than ours alone.

author: william_wordsworth
text:
O! how could ye give up so great an enemy,
 When the time came for us all to pay him back?
 What madness! what folly was in your brains then?
 To put off such a bloody business till now?
 We have done nothing but wait, since we can see,
 That he had more than enough, and more than knew,
 And much better store of means than we have too:
 Nor shall we do aught but die, or else prove
 Some things worse than death, while he grows rich, while we
 Die like dogs, if we

author: william_wordsworth
text:
O thou whose light on earth is dying fast,
 And whom the night-clouds o'erhead are hiding vast,
 O Night! now hast thou conquered at last,
 The Day's bright lustre hath no more to boast.
